Females of the Tank goby (Glossogobius giuris) attain a maximum total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], a value that represents an asymptotic size rarely exceeded in natural populations. This ultimate length is notably large among Indo-Pacific gobiids and is typically reached only after several years of sustained growth in productive estuarine habitats. Field surveys across the lower Mekong delta have confirmed that individuals exceeding this size are almost invariably females, consistent with the pronounced sexual size dimorphism that characterizes this species.

Puberty in Glossogobius giuris is marked by the onset of gonadal recrudescence and is reached when individuals achieve a total length of approximately 9 centimeters [Lp = approximately 9 centimeters]. The corresponding wet weight at this developmental milestone is 6.4 grams [Wwp = 6.4 grams], a body mass that reflects the minimum somatic investment required before reproductive physiology is activated. These values, derived from histological examination of gonad tissue in wild-caught specimens from Philippine brackish lagoons, align closely with allometric predictions based on the species length-weight relationship.

At a sustained water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], laboratory-held neonates emerge from the egg capsule at just 5 days [ab = 5 days] following fertilization. The hatchlings, which are initially lecithotrophic yolk-sac larvae, have a wet weight of 0.00016 grams [Wwb = 0.00016 grams] upon eclosion, a remarkably tiny birth mass that is consistent with the small egg dimensions documented in related goby species. This abbreviated embryonic period, combined with the diminutive size of the prolarvae, suggests a high-risk early life strategy that relies on rapid yolk absorption and the timely commencement of exogenous feeding.

Under identical thermal conditions of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for this goby is 7 years [am = 7 years], a lifespan that is relatively extended for a species of its moderate adult body size. Females that survive to senescence can achieve an ultimate wet weight of 1266 grams [Wwi = 1266 grams], a massive increase from the birth mass that underscores the species impressive capacity for somatic growth in productive coastal environments. This substantial asymptotic mass, which is more than seven million times the neonatal weight, places Glossogobius giuris among the heavier members of its genus.

Reproductive output in this species is substantial, with mature females producing approximately 918 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 918 eggs per day] during peak spawning periods under stable conditions at 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This high fecundity, sustained over a breeding season that often spans several months, compensates for the vulnerability of the tiny, free-drifting larvae. The species benthic, nest-guarding adults exhibit iteroparous reproduction, and the combination of small neonatal mass and high daily egg production reflects an opportunistic life-history strategy well-suited to variable tropical estuaries.
